phases.name: Convoy Placement
phases.description: NATO places convoys on the map.
phases.content: During each turn, NATO will receive one Convoy and may receive a Mediterranean Convoy. The NATO player may then select from any of the counter types available (except the Fast Convoy, which enters via event only). All Convoys are then placed on the map in a port in the United States.
phases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** Convoys are the war NATO has to win at sea. The Convoy Placement Phase (3.2.1) abstracts the steady flow of US logistics into Western Europe by putting one fresh Convoy on the board in a US port every single turn. Without that flow, the European front runs out of fuel and ammunition and the Soviet army keeps advancing.

**What is at stake.** The Convoy *type* is determined by the Reinforcement Track; whichever counter the track shows enters play this turn (3.2.1). The Fast Convoy enters only via card event and never appears on the track. The Mediterranean Convoy is a separate, scenario-keyed extra placement, not a substitute for the Atlantic one.

**Gotchas.** New players forget that the Convoy type is fixed by the Reinforcement Track, not a free choice. What you control is *where* the Convoy is placed (any US port) and how quickly an escort can be assembled to move it. The Med Convoy is easy to miss entirely on turns when the scenario card schedules it. Check the scenario setup every turn.

**Synergies.** This phase pairs tightly with later TF formation actions and with NATO escort allocation. Drop a Convoy in a US port that has spare escort capacity and the TF can sail next Ships event with a full ASW screen. Plan the Convoy type around the cards in hand; a Fast Convoy event becomes very strong when there is room in the queue to chain a fast move with a high-OPS card.

**Example beat.** Turn 3 opens with Convoys already pinned in the East and a Soviet Foxtrot pack waiting in East 3. The Reinforcement Track shows a Materiel Convoy; NATO places it in New York, intending to escort it south through the Mid zones rather than running the gauntlet a third time. The Soviet player sees the placement, knows the Materiel value is highest, and starts moving subs west to intercept. The port choice made here in five seconds drove the whole turn.
phases.coachContentShort: Pick the Convoy type with the next two turns in mind, not just this one: an Amphib with no landing target wastes a slot a Materiel could fill (3.2.1). Vary the type and entry port turn to turn so the Soviet player cannot pre-position a sub pack on the same Sea Zone twice. Check the scenario for a Mediterranean Convoy on the current turn before you finish the phase, it is a separate, easy-to-miss placement.

phases.name: Reinforcement
phases.content:
Depending on the set-up chosen, each side has several units that will become available during the game. These include Amphibious units for both sides, RORSATs for the Soviets, and Carrier Battle Groups for NATO.

During the Reinforcement Phase the units arriving are placed on the map. All reinforcements arrive in any port belonging to the owning nation. Soviet RORSATs are placed in the Tyuratam box.
phases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The Reinforcement Phase (3.2.2) is the scheduled drumbeat of new hulls and air units arriving from each side's strategic reserve. It models the gradual buildup of forces that were either steaming from home waters or being released from other theatres, and it is the only routine way new Carrier Battle Groups, Amphibious units, and RORSATs enter play.

**What is at stake.** Where you place a reinforcement determines what it can do this turn. NATO reinforcements arrive in any NATO port (3.2.2), so an arriving carrier can dock in the UK to threaten the Norwegian Sea or in Norfolk to escort Convoys. Soviet reinforcements arrive in any Soviet port, with the hard exception that RORSATs are placed in the Tyuratam box rather than on the map (3.2.2). Amphibs land here too, and their port choice locks in the landing arc for the next Ships event.

**Gotchas.** Reinforcements arrive in port, not at sea, so they cannot move or shoot until a Ships or Fast event. A Soviet player who reinforces an Amphib intending to land this turn must remember the landing process needs a marker placed during Ships, then an actual landing on the *next* Ships beat (8.1.1). RORSATs in Tyuratam are off the map and contribute nothing to detection until the Soviet player spends an OPS to deploy them. Players sometimes forget the scenario's reinforcement schedule entirely and discover a counter still in the box at end of game.

**Synergies.** A new NATO carrier in a UK port pairs with a same-turn Strike action against a Soviet airfield, since the Ships event will give it intrinsic detection (5.1.5.3) in the right Sea Zone. A Soviet Amphib reinforcing into Kola pairs with the Soviet Overland Troops to Norway sequence (8.1.3) to threaten Trondheim from two axes.

**Example beat.** Turn 5 arrives, the schedule places a CBG in NATO's queue and a Tarawa-class Amphib in the Soviet queue. NATO drops the CBG in Faslane to put it one move from North 5-6 next Ships event. The Soviet player puts the Amphib in Polyarny so it can move into North 9-10 and mark Landing for Trondheim on the same turn.
phases.coachContentShort: Place reinforcements with their first action already planned: a CBG in Faslane threatens the Norwegian Sea next Ships event, a CBG in Norfolk escorts Convoys (3.2.2). Soviet Amphibs must mark Landing during one Ships event and resolve the landing on the next, so a same-turn invasion requires arriving in a port adjacent to the target arc. RORSATs go to Tyuratam and contribute nothing until a later OPS deploys them.

phases.name: Operations Phase
phases.description: Open-ended phase: players spend OPS points from cards in any order. See the Actions tab for the full action catalog.
phases.content:
a) The Soviet player selects a card to play for its Operations Points and records the number on the Operations Point Record Track with the Soviet marker.

b) The NATO player selects a card to play for its Operations Points and records the number on the Operations Point Record Track with the NATO marker.

c) The Soviet player plays the first Operations Point to perform an action or Passes (4.2).

d) The NATO player plays an Operations Point to perform an action or Passes (4.2).

e) Continue alternating through c. and d. until no Operations Points remain.

Look for events on the Operations Point Record Track: **Fast**, **Repair**, **Ships**, and **Next Day**. These trigger when both players' Operations Points marker reaches or passes the box and takes effect immediately after the current action is resolved.

Open the [Actions tab](tab:actions) for the full action catalog with OPS costs.

subPhases.name: OPS Event — Fast (ignored Day 2)
subPhases.description: Fast Task Forces get a free movement beat. Skipped entirely on Day 2.
subPhases.content: If it is not Day Two: Fast Task Forces may move one Sea Zone (they may not perform ASW). If it is Day Two, ignore this event. Resolve as per the Ships event, ignoring steps 2 and 4, and applying only to Fast TFs and zones they occupy.
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The Fast event (4.2.1.1) gives the navies with high-speed nuclear-powered or gas-turbine task forces an extra movement beat. Historically a Fast TF could cross a sea area in roughly half the time of a Slow one, so the game grants them a separate, earlier movement opportunity that the rest of the fleet does not get.

**What is at stake.** Only Fast TFs move during this event, and they move *one* Sea Zone (4.2.1.1). They cannot conduct ASW during Fast, which is a deliberate constraint: this is a positioning beat, not a combat beat. The event is *ignored entirely on Day Two* in the standard game and does not exist at all in the smaller scenarios that use the compressed OPS track. Check the day before you resolve.

**Gotchas.** Skipping the Fast event on Day Two is the single most common omission new players make. The event card-trigger walks through steps 1, 3, 5, and 6 of the Ships event sequence (4.2.1.3), explicitly skipping step 2 (detection degrade) and step 4 (Spent removal), so Fast TFs that do not move during this beat do *not* drop from Good to Poor, which preserves their detection going into the later Ships event. Fast also follows on-patrol reaction rules: enemy On-Patrol submarines and MP can react to Fast TF movement just like during a Ships event (5.2.3, 5.3.4.1). Fast TFs may not amphibious-land during Fast, since Fast forbids the substitute actions that Ships permits.

**Synergies.** Fast pairs with NATO Carrier Battle Groups built around US carriers (which roll two intrinsic detection dice, 5.1.5.3) since the early move puts them in striking range one beat ahead of slower Soviet TFs. Soviet Fast TFs are rare but use the event to thread the Norwegian Sea and threaten Convoys before NATO can respond.

**Example beat.** Day One, Fast event triggers. NATO's US-1 CBG (Fast) in North 3-4 moves one zone to North 5-6, picks up a Good detection on a Soviet TF already loitering there, and gets free intrinsic detection rolls (5.1.5.3). The Soviet TF that did not move keeps its Good marker because step 2 was skipped. NATO now opens the real Ships event with a fully developed targeting picture.
subPhases.coachContentShort: Skip Fast entirely on Day Two, this is the single most common omission (4.2.1.1). On Day One, every Fast TF may move one Sea Zone but may not conduct ASW: it is a positioning beat, not a combat beat. The event walks only steps 1, 3, 5, and 6 of the Ships sequence, so detection degrade and Spent removal are skipped, which preserves your Fast TFs' detection going into the real Ships event.

subPhases.name: OPS Event — Repair
subPhases.description: Remove one hit from every damaged facility on the map.
subPhases.content: Remove one hit from each damaged facility on the map and then check to see if the facility is now lightly damaged or no longer damaged (2.3.8.5).
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The Repair event (4.2.1.2) is the passive recovery channel for damaged facilities. Bases get hit constantly in BWN, between cruise missile salvos, amphibious raids, and event cards, and without an automatic recovery beat the side absorbing the punishment would lose airfields and ports faster than it could rebuild them.

**What is at stake.** The Repair event removes *one* hit from every damaged facility on the map (4.2.1.2), then rechecks each facility against the damage thresholds in 2.3.8.5. A facility at Heavy can drop to Light, and a facility at Light can return to undamaged. This is a freebie: no OPS spent, no die roll required.

**Gotchas.** Players forget that the recheck against 2.3.8.5 happens *every time* a hit is removed. Each turn also passively removes two hits per damaged facility (one per OPS card played, per 2.3.8.5), so the Repair event is an *additional* hit removal on top of the baseline two. Some new players believe Repair is the only repair mechanism and underbuild their action economy because of it. The Repair *action* (5.4.1) is a separate, OPS-spending action that can additionally accelerate recovery, and is worth pairing with Repair on the same turn when a critical base is at Heavy. Also, the Soviet side has facilities too. Players sometimes mentally apply Repair only to NATO and miss that a hit comes off Tyuratam, Kola, Polyarny, and so on.

**Synergies.** Repair pairs with the Repair action (5.4.1) on a key base where you absolutely need an airfield back online for a Strike next turn. It also pairs negatively with attrition strategies: a Soviet player who only puts one hit on a NATO airfield per turn gives that base back at the Repair event and the OPS pass-through, and may want to commit to a multi-hit strike instead.

**Example beat.** Faslane is at Light damage with three hits when the Repair event triggers. The event removes one hit, dropping the total to two. The owning player then rechecks 2.3.8.5: Faslane no longer meets the Light damage threshold, the marker comes off, and the British Sturgeons based there can now fly Strike again from Day Two onward.
subPhases.coachContentShort: Repair removes one hit from every damaged facility on the map for free, then rechecks each against 2.3.8.5 to see if Heavy drops to Light or Light goes undamaged (4.2.1.2). Pair it with the Repair action (5.4.1) the same turn when a critical base sits at Heavy and you need it back online for next turn's Strike. Remember the Soviet side has facilities too, hits come off Tyuratam, Kola, and Polyarny as well as NATO bases.

subPhases.name: OPS Event — Ships
subPhases.description: The big movement beat. TF movement, detection degrade, RORSATs, spent removal, F-v-F combat, intrinsic detection.
subPhases.content:
1. Move Task Forces.

Both sides move all Task Forces according to the movement rules (5.1.3). The Soviet player moves all Task Forces first, followed by NATO within each detection category.

Task Forces may prepare for an Amphibious Landing by marking themselves with the 'Amphibious Landing' marker. For each that does, roll a free Task Force Detection roll (6.1). Task Forces already marked with an 'Amphibious Landing' marker may resolve their landing, and then remove the marker. If they do so they may not move.

If a Task Force moves into or from a zone with a friendly nuclear submarine which is not Spent or On Patrol, the submarine may join the Task Force so long as it is the only submarine with the Task Force.

Instead of moving a Task Force, it may conduct Anti-Submarine Warfare in its current zone (7.2.2).

Units marked as 'On Patrol' may react to enemy Task Force movement (5.2.3, 5.3.4.1, 5.3.4.2).

Air Units marked 'On Patrol' may move with a Task Force that just moved so long as they have the range to operate there (i.e. they must remain within range of their base).

2. Degrade existing Task Force detections that were not placed in step 1 (if they have an Amphibious Landing marker, do not degrade the Detection level). All Good detections are reduced to Poor detections and all Poor detections are removed. See (6.1.1.3) for the effect of downgrading Task Force Detection levels.

3. Roll for Task Force Detection with each RORSAT on the map which shares a Sea Zone with one or more enemy Task Force(s).

4. Remove 'Spent' markers from all non-MP Air Units (except for Air Units at a base with Heavy damage).

5. Resolve Fighter vs Fighter combat due to the movement of Task Forces (7.1.3).

6. Resolve Interception and CAP response to intrinsic detection units and then resolve their searches.
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The Ships event (4.2.1.3) is the main movement and detection beat of the turn, the heartbeat that makes BWN a Cold War naval game rather than an action puzzle. Task Forces only move at Fast or Ships events, so every threat trajectory, every interception, every detection roll lives or dies on what gets resolved here.

**What is at stake.** Six sub-steps run in strict order. Move Task Forces (Soviet first, by detection category), then degrade detections that were not placed in step 1, then RORSAT searches, then remove Spent markers from non-MP Air Units, then resolve Fighter vs Fighter combat triggered by movement, then resolve intrinsic detection (4.2.1.3). The order matters because each step's result feeds the next: degraded detections in step 2 change the dice math for the RORSAT searches in step 3.

**Gotchas.** The order is the trap. New players move all their TFs and then forget the detection degrade entirely, or run the RORSAT search before the degrade and over-detect. Other common misses: detections not placed during step 1 have Good downgraded to Poor and Poor removed in step 2, *unless* the TF holds an Amphibious Landing marker (4.2.1.3). A TF that moves into a zone with a friendly On-Patrol or non-Spent nuclear sub may pick up that sub (one max per TF). On-Patrol enemy units may react to TF movement (5.2.3, 5.3.4.1, 5.3.4.2), and a TF may substitute ASW in its current zone for movement (7.2.2). RORSATs do not get a free detection when moved into a zone with enemy TFs; their detection roll only happens during step 3.

**Synergies.** Ships pairs with everything. Carrier Battle Groups gain free intrinsic detection (5.1.5.3) in step 6. On-Patrol Air Units may move *with* a moving TF if range permits, threading CAP coverage across zones. The Amphibious Landing marker is placed during step 1 and lets a TF skip the degrade in step 2, protecting Good detection for the landing roll next event.

**Example beat.** Soviet moves first within Undetected category, sliding a Foxtrot pack from East 3 into East 2 where it intends to ambush a NATO Convoy. NATO then moves its Good-detected CBG one zone north. In step 2, the stationary Soviet TF in Mid 2 drops from Good to Poor. Step 3, a RORSAT in North 5-6 rolls for detection on the NATO CBG passing through, scores a 9, places Good. Step 5, NATO Phantoms triggered by the CBG move resolve F-v-F with Soviet MiG-23s on patrol. The whole turn just pivoted on one Ships event.
subPhases.coachContentShort: Run the six sub-steps in strict order, the order is the trap (4.2.1.3): move (Soviet first by detection category), degrade detections not placed in step 1, RORSATs, Spent removal, F-v-F, then intrinsic detection. A detection that was not placed or refreshed during step 1 drops Good to Poor and Poor to Undetected, unless the TF carries an Amphibious Landing marker, which protects detection for next-event's landing roll. A friendly nuclear sub already on patrol in the zone may join a moving TF, one sub per TF max.

subPhases.name: OPS Event — Next Day (ignored Day 2)
subPhases.description: Both players play their second OPS card and advance to Day 2. Skipped on Day 2 itself.
subPhases.content:
Both players play their second (and last) card of the turn for its Operations Points, exactly as per (3.2.3), adding the number of Operations Points still unspent to the total available to you.

Advance the Day marker to 'Day Two' then continue play.
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** Next Day (4.2.1.4) is the hinge between the two halves of a standard BWN turn. Each player plays a second OPS card, accumulates the new total with any unspent points carried over, and the Day marker flips to Day Two. This structure builds card balance around a known total of four card plays per turn while still permitting a player to hold OPS in reserve.

**What is at stake.** Both players play their second (and last) OPS card of the turn exactly as in 3.2.3, *adding* unspent Day One OPS to the new total (4.2.1.4). Then the Day marker advances. The event is ignored entirely on Day Two itself, and the smaller scenarios that use the compressed OPS track have no Next Day event at all per the Scenario Book.

**Gotchas.** The most expensive miss is forgetting that *unspent* OPS carry over. A NATO player who finishes Day One with 2 OPS unspent and plays a 3 OPS card on Day Two has 5 OPS for Day Two, not 3. This is intentional and lets you bank for a big action like a multi-leg Strike. Some cards say things like 'during this card play' or 'until the end of this card play': per the rules clarification on 4.1, this is intended to mean 'during the day that this event is used', so a SOSUS Sabotage played on Day One can be triggered on Day Two and last all of Day Two. Also, the Next Day event does not let you draw new cards; the second OPS card comes from your current hand. Card draw happens in End of Turn (3.3.5).

**Synergies.** Next Day pairs with the standard plan of holding a high-OPS card for Day Two when the Soviet player has shown their full hand strength, or with banking 1-2 OPS unspent on Day One to make a Day Two Strike possible. It also pairs with Reaction Event cards held in hand, since those cost no OPS and can be sprung in either day.

**Example beat.** Day One ends with both markers at the Next Day box and NATO holding 1 unspent OPS. NATO plays a 4 OPS card on Day Two for a new total of 5. Soviet, having budgeted to attack a Convoy that just appeared in Mid 3, plays its remaining 5 OPS card. Day Two opens with both sides flush and the Soviet plan to mass Backfires hinges on getting a Bear D detection before NATO can fly fresh Phantoms forward.
subPhases.coachContentShort: Unspent OPS carry over: a player ending Day One with 2 unspent who plays a 3 OPS card on Day Two has 5 OPS, not 3 (4.2.1.4). Skip this event entirely on Day Two itself. No new cards are drawn here, the second OPS card comes from your existing hand and the card draw is in the End of Turn phase (3.3.5), so plan your hand around four total card plays per turn.

phases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The Operations Phase (3.2.3, 4.1, 4.2) is the engine of the game. Each side reveals an OPS card, then alternates spending points one action at a time, with Soviet going first. This back-and-forth, action-by-action structure (rather than IGOUGO) is what creates the tense bidding tempo where a player must constantly weigh spending now versus saving for a reaction or a powerful card play later.

**What is at stake.** Card selection comes first, and the order matters: Soviet plays a card before NATO, so NATO sees the Soviet OPS number before committing its own (4.1). That single piece of information drives the whole turn. A low Soviet card invites NATO to play big and crowd the action economy; a high Soviet card is a signal that the Soviet player is planning a major operation and NATO should hold an OPS reserve to react.

**Gotchas.** The phase has many small rules players miss. A Pass is only legal when you have *fewer* OPS than your opponent (4.2). You cannot Pass to bait. Use-when-active options like playing a Reaction Event, returning an On-Patrol Air Unit, or drawing a card if you have under three (4.2.2 and 4.2.3) are free and slot in *between* your actions, not as actions. The top Operations Event on a card in hand costs two extra OPS to play (4.2.2.5), often forgotten. And the OPS Track events (Fast, Repair, Ships, Next Day) trigger when *both* markers have reached or passed the box, resolved immediately after the current action (4.2.1), not at some indeterminate later beat.

**Synergies.** OPS card play interlocks with every other system. A high-OPS card lets you stack Move plus Strike plus Patrol in one turn. A low card with a strong event you intend to fire as a reaction is sometimes better than a high card with a weak event. Watch the Track: place your last action so the marker stops *just* past a Ships event you want or *just* short of one you do not.

**Example beat.** Soviet plays a 4 OPS card; NATO sees it and plays a 5. Soviet spends OPS 1 to move an Echo into East 3. NATO spends OPS 1 to fly a P-3 ASW from Lajes. Soviet OPS 2 triggers the Ships event mid-turn, both TFs degrade, and NATO suddenly has to re-plan because the Backfire raid it was building toward just lost its Good detection.
phases.coachContentShort: Card selection drives the turn: Soviet plays first, so NATO sees the Soviet OPS total before committing its own (4.1). A Pass is legal only when you have fewer OPS than your opponent, you cannot Pass to bait (4.2). Track the OPS marker against the Fast, Repair, Ships, and Next Day boxes: events trigger when both markers reach or pass, resolving immediately after the current action completes (4.2.1).

phases.name: End of Turn
phases.description: Cleanup, invasions, first strike, weather, event cards, then advance turn.

subPhases.name: a) Turn Clean-Up
subPhases.description: Return interceptors / on-patrol MP to base; remove spent markers; choose to remove sub on-patrol markers.
subPhases.content:
a) Fighters on Interception missions and 'On Patrol' MP units may return to base. **If a zone contains Fighter units of both sides, all Air Units return to base.**

b) Remove all 'Spent' markers (except for Air Units at a heavily damaged base).

c) Choose to remove 'On Patrol' markers on Submarine Units, or to retain them. Submarines with 'On Patrol' markers can only react to enemy units.
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** Turn Clean-Up (3.3.1) resets the Air Unit and Submarine posture for the next turn. Without it, Spent markers and Interception placements would accumulate indefinitely and Air Units would be permanently grounded after one mission, which is not the operational reality the game is modeling.

**What is at stake.** Three steps. First, Fighters that flew Interception missions and 'On Patrol' MP units *may* return to base, with one hard exception: if a Sea Zone contains Fighter units of *both* sides, all Air Units in that zone return to base (3.3.1a). Second, remove all Spent markers, except for Air Units at a heavily damaged base (3.3.1b). Third, decide whether to remove the On-Patrol marker from each Submarine, or keep it; subs with On-Patrol can only react to enemy units (3.3.1c).

**Gotchas.** The forced-return rule in step a is the trap. Players assume Air Units always choose to return to base, but the rule is *may* in the normal case and *must* in the mixed-Fighter zone case. If you parked Phantoms on patrol in North 5-6 and a Soviet MiG-23 ends the turn there too, both sides' Air Units fly home, even if you wanted to hold position. The Heavy-damage exception in step b is often missed: an airbase under Heavy damage keeps its Spent Air Units Spent, which can lock down a Soviet wing for an entire turn until Repair fires. The submarine choice in step c is genuine: leaving On-Patrol on a sub keeps it in a reactive posture and unable to take active actions next turn.

**Synergies.** Clean-Up pairs with the Repair event and Repair action: if you can lift a base from Heavy to Light during the OPS phase, that base's Air Units will get their Spent markers removed at Clean-Up. It pairs negatively with Strike actions late on Day Two, since aircraft that come back Spent will still drop Spent at Clean-Up regardless.

**Example beat.** Turn 6 Clean-Up. NATO's F-14s on interception in Mid 3 return to USS Nimitz, free. Soviet MiG-23s on patrol in North 5-6 share the zone with British Sea Harriers, so both sides' fighters are forced back to base. Spent markers come off everyone except a Tu-22M wing at Olenya, which is at Heavy damage and stays Spent. The Soviet player keeps an On-Patrol marker on a Victor III in Mid 2 to react to NATO's convoy run next turn.
subPhases.coachContentShort: The forced-return rule is the trap: if a Sea Zone holds Fighter units of both sides at end of turn, all Air Units in that zone fly home, even if you wanted to hold position (3.3.1a). Spent markers come off everyone except Air Units at a Heavy-damaged base, which can lock down a wing until Repair fires (3.3.1b). The submarine On-Patrol choice in step c is real: leaving the marker on keeps the sub reactive but blocks active actions next turn.

subPhases.name: b) Invasions
subPhases.description: Resolve Denmark / Norway tracks, then war-track adjustments and capture rolls.
subPhases.content:
a) Resolve the Invasion War Tracks (Denmark and Norway).

b) Increase the Danish Strait Mining level if no Soviet troops ever landed in Denmark.

c) Roll to clear the Danish Strait of mines if the War marker is in a relevant box.

d) Select a bonus if Norway has surrendered.

e) Remove submarines if required by the Invasion Tracks.

Calculate War Track changes for Convoys and Soviet advances, then remove submarines, capture facilities and resolve NATO nuclear weapon usage if required by the War Tracks.

Remove **3 hits** on the Europe South War Track and on the Norway and Denmark Invasion Tracks.
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The Invasions subsection (3.3.2) is where naval action gets paid out into the European land war. Soviet troops landed via amphibious operation or delivered overland push the Invasion Tracks (Norway and Denmark); the war tracks for Europe North and South advance one box west; NATO strikes against Soviet troops can cancel an advance. This is the bridge between the at-sea game and the ground war the game is ultimately about.

**What is at stake.** Five steps in order (3.3.2): resolve the Invasion War Tracks (Denmark, Norway), then Danish Strait mining changes (8.4.2), then a possible mine-clearing roll (8.4.2.1), then a Norwegian surrender bonus selection (8.4.3), then sub removal required by the tracks. After that, compute War Track changes for Convoys and Soviet advances, capture facilities, resolve NATO nuke usage if triggered (8.2.4), and remove 3 hits each from Europe South, Norway, and Denmark tracks.

**Gotchas.** Order matters and the bookkeeping is dense. The 3-hit removal at the end is mandatory; hits that did not reach the 3-cancel threshold disappear and do not accumulate to next turn. NATO Strikes against Soviet troops in Denmark may fly from either the Baltic or the North Sea, since both border the relevant troop locations. NATO can land troops in Northern Norway even if the Norway Track is in the South, but still resolves resistance with the friendly-troops modifier. NATO nukes fire *automatically* when Soviet troops enter the Ruhr box and the Soviet player holds fewer than 2 FSPs (or fewer than 4 if chemicals were used). It is not optional, it is not a choice; the trigger is hardcoded in 8.2.4.

**Synergies.** This subsection pairs with the amphibious landing actions earlier in the turn: troops delivered into Norway show up here and may double-advance if their count is double the Troops Needed value. It pairs with the Danish Strait clearing rule (8.4.2.1): clearing the Strait immediately mines French, British, Belgian, and Dutch ports as Heavy, which can ruin NATO's Atlantic logistics in a single beat.

**Example beat.** End of Turn 7. Soviet has 5 troops on the Norway Invasion Track; the current box requires a Troops Needed of 4. Since 5 >= 4, the track advances one box. Since 5 < 8 (2 x 4), there is no double advance. NATO had landed 2 hits on Soviet troops earlier in the turn; 3 hits are needed to cancel a War Track advance, so the hits come off at end of turn and the advance stands. Norway has not yet surrendered, no bonus chosen. The Soviet player privately resolves whether to mass an Amphib next turn or push overland.
subPhases.coachContentShort: The 3-hit removal on Europe South, Norway, and Denmark at the end is mandatory and wipes any hits that did not reach the 3-cancel threshold (3.3.2), so partial Strikes are wasted. The NATO Ruhr nuke is automatic, not a choice: it fires when Soviet troops enter the Ruhr box with fewer than 2 FSPs in reserve, or fewer than 4 if chemicals were used (8.2.4). Clearing the Danish Strait immediately Heavy-mines NATO Atlantic ports (8.4.2.1), which can ruin convoy logistics in one beat.

subPhases.name: c) First Strike
subPhases.description: On a First Strike turn, award FSP if Soviet SSBN payload is staged in First Strike zones.
subPhases.content: If the current turn has a **First Strike icon**, award the Soviet player **1 First Strike Point** if at least **6 SSBN Payload value** are in First Strike zones (ignore the Arctic and the Bastion).
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The First Strike subsection (3.3.3) is the periodic dividend the Soviet player earns for keeping SSBN Payload value forward-deployed in First Strike zones. The whole boomer subsystem in BWN exists to pressure the Soviet player into a risk-reward decision: park in the safe Bastion and forfeit some FSP income, or sortie out and earn but expose the SSBNs to hunting.

**What is at stake.** If the current turn shows a First Strike icon, count Soviet SSBN Payload value in First Strike zones, ignoring the Arctic and the Bastion (3.3.3, 9.1.1). If the total is 6 or more, the Soviet player gains 1 First Strike Point. That FSP can then be spent on the ASAT System, on stepping up a strategic reserve unit, on triggering Nuclear Weapons at Sea (3 FSPs, 10.2), on battlefield nuclear weapons (5 FSPs), or on blocking NATO's Ruhr nuke trigger (2 or 4 FSPs).

**Gotchas.** The 6-Payload threshold is a *total* across all First Strike zones, not per zone. You can sum 3 Payload in one FS zone with 3 in another to clear the bar. The Arctic and the Bastion do *not* count for this end-of-turn award. They have their own roles: the Bastion is the safe haven where SSBNs earn from second-strike-only cards, the Arctic earns from regular First Strike cards. Only on-station units count; SSBNs in transit through a First Strike zone but not yet on station do not contribute. Cards that have their own First Strike Payload thresholds (like the First Strike Soviet event card) use different math, so do not conflate the card and the end-of-turn award.

**Synergies.** This subsection pairs with sortie planning during the OPS phase. A Soviet player who pushes a Typhoon plus escort out of the Bastion into a First Strike zone on Day One sets up the award here on a First-Strike-icon turn. It pairs with the Soviet Spies action (9.3) which can auto-succeed evasion rolls in a single zone, protecting a vulnerable on-station SSBN.

**Example beat.** Turn 8, First Strike icon on the turn track. Soviet has a Typhoon (Payload 8) on station in North 9-10 and a Delta IV (Payload 4) under the Arctic Ice. The Arctic does not count. Only the Typhoon's 8 counts, which exceeds the 6 threshold, so the Soviet player gains 1 FSP. The Soviet player tucks the FSP toward the 3 they need for Nuclear Weapons at Sea on a future turn.
subPhases.coachContentShort: Sum Soviet SSBN Payload across all First Strike zones (not the Arctic, not the Bastion): hit 6 total on a First-Strike-icon turn and earn 1 FSP (3.3.3, 9.1.1). Only on-station SSBNs count, payload in transit through a zone does not contribute. Pair sortie planning during OPS with the icon on the turn track: a Typhoon pushed out of the Bastion on Day One sets up the award here, and Spies (9.3) can auto-succeed an evasion roll to protect a vulnerable boat.

subPhases.name: d) Weather
subPhases.description: Remove all Bad Weather markers and roll fresh weather per zone.
subPhases.content:
Remove all Weather markers and roll for weather (3.4) in each Weather Zone on the map.

### Procedure (§3.4)

First remove all Bad Weather markers from the map. Then, roll one die for weather in each Weather Zone (West, Mid, East, North, Med) and use the appropriate table printed on the map. If the result is a number, roll that many dice and place Bad Weather in all Sea Zones with the matching number within that Weather Zone — some areas have more than one zone with the same number (e.g. Barents Sea and the Bastion are both 9–10).

A Sea Zone can only have a Bad Weather effect once a turn. If a rolled zone already has a Bad Weather marker, **ignore the dice which rolled the same number** — that die roll generates no further weather effect. Land bordering or within a zone with Bad Weather also has Bad Weather. Some land is affected by multiple Sea Zones.

*Example*: The North Weather Zone is rolled for and the result is an 8 which is '2' — two dice are rolled — 7 and 8. The first Bad Weather marker is placed into North 7-8 to account for the 7. The 8 is ignored because it's a duplicate result.
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** Weather (3.3.4, 3.4) re-rolls the operational environment each turn. The North Atlantic is rarely calm in the relevant operational latitudes, and the game models Bad Weather as a per-Sea-Zone state that slows Task Force movement, complicates landings, and degrades detection. Without a weather phase the game would feel sterile and over-deterministic.

**What is at stake.** Remove all Bad Weather markers first. Then roll one die for each Weather Zone (West, Mid, East, North, Med) and consult the table on the map. If the result is a number, roll that many dice and place Bad Weather in matching-numbered Sea Zones within that Weather Zone (3.4). A Sea Zone can only have Bad Weather once per turn; duplicate die results are ignored. Land bordering or within a Bad Weather Sea Zone also has Bad Weather, and some land is affected by multiple Sea Zones.

**Gotchas.** The duplicate-ignore rule is the easy miss. If you roll a 7 and an 8 in the North zone but North 7-8 is one combined Sea Zone, the 8 generates no further weather effect because the zone is already marked. The Barents Sea and the Bastion share 9-10, so a single roll can put weather on both. Bad Weather does not stop a TF from moving out of a *port*: leaving a port ignores Bad Weather per 5.1.3.6, a frequent surprise. A TF starting a turn in Bad Weather still processes the Ships event normally, but cannot leave the zone on that beat; place a Moved marker instead and it moves on the *next* movement opportunity (5.1.3.1). On-Patrol reactions still follow standard rules; they only trigger when an enemy actually moves into or through the area.

**Synergies.** Weather pairs with amphibious landing timing. A landing into a Bad Weather zone gives the defender no free detection on the landing TF (because the TF's detection cannot be improved while marked Landing), but the landing is hard work and takes longer. ASW rolls in Bad Weather lose a die (the seas are noisy, thermal layers are scrambled), which favors the side relying on stealth.

**Example beat.** End of Turn 5. All weather markers come off. North Weather Zone rolls an 8, which reads '2' on the map table. Two dice: 7 and 8. North 7-8 is one Sea Zone, so the first die places Bad Weather there; the second die is a duplicate and ignored. The Soviet player's planned Backfire run from Olenya through North 7-8 now has to either route around or accept reduced effect.
subPhases.coachContentShort: Bad Weather places per Sea Zone, and each zone can only have one marker per turn, so duplicate die results within a Weather Zone are ignored (3.4). Leaving a port ignores Bad Weather (5.1.3.6), a frequent surprise for both sides. A TF that starts a turn in Bad Weather processes the Ships event normally but cannot leave the zone on that beat, place a Moved marker and it moves on the next opportunity (5.1.3.1).

subPhases.name: e) Event Cards
subPhases.description: Hold (NATO 2 / Soviet 1) or discard; then draw back up to 5.
subPhases.content:
Choose to hold up to **two cards** (NATO) or **one card** (Soviet) and discard all other cards.

Then, draw up to **5 cards** in-hand. If you held cards, you'll draw fewer new cards.

*Note*: Holding cards is not mandatory.
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The Event Cards subsection (3.3.5) is the deck cycle. Each player keeps a hand of up to 5 cards, and at end of turn chooses how aggressively to refresh. The asymmetric retention limits, NATO holds up to 2, Soviet holds 1, reflect the design's view that NATO has a deeper bench of useful reaction events while Soviet plays a hotter, higher-variance set.

**What is at stake.** Choose to hold up to 2 cards (NATO) or up to 1 card (Soviet), discard the rest, then draw back up to 5 in hand (3.3.5). Holding is *not* mandatory; you can discard your whole hand if you do not like any of it. If you held cards, your new draws will be fewer in number to compensate.

**Gotchas.** Holding cards is a real decision and most players under-hold. A strong Reaction Event in hand is often worth keeping into the next turn because Reaction events cost no OPS to fire and let you punch outside your action budget. The asymmetry is the trap for the Soviet player: holding *one* card means the Soviet hand cycles faster on average, so keep the *right* one. Cards drawn at end of turn are random; you cannot plan a specific combo across turns, only set up the conditions for one. Also, OPS cards in your hand are not the same as Event-played cards: cards played for OPS are discarded after the day they were played in, and event-played cards may track separately depending on the card text.

**Synergies.** Holding pairs with anticipated next-turn states. If you know the next turn has a First Strike icon, hold any card that boosts SSBN sortie capability or detection. If you expect a major NATO Strike next turn, hold a Soviet reaction card that helps SAM defense.

**What the player can influence.** This is one of the rare end-of-turn beats with real player choice. Treat the hold-or-discard decision as carefully as an OPS card selection. Look at the next turn's icons (First Strike, Convoy Surge) and at the current board state; the right card to hold changes turn to turn.

**Example beat.** End of Turn 6. NATO looks at its 5-card hand: 4 OPS Spruance, 3 OPS Determined Attack, 2 OPS Tomahawk, 2 OPS Whitecloud, 1 OPS routine. Soviet ASAT is in Tyuratam blocking Whitecloud, so NATO discards that one. NATO holds Determined Attack and Tomahawk as Day Two plays for next turn, discards the rest, and draws 3 new cards back up to 5.
subPhases.coachContentShort: Hold up to 2 cards (NATO) or 1 card (Soviet), discard the rest, then draw back to 5 (3.3.5). Most players under-hold: a strong Reaction Event is often worth keeping because Reactions cost no OPS and let you punch outside your action budget. Read the next turn's icons before you decide, hold a Whitecloud or sortie-boost card when the next turn shows First Strike, hold SAM-defense when you expect a NATO Strike.

subPhases.name: f) Next Turn
subPhases.description: Advance the Turn Marker and roll for Soviet ASAT removal.
subPhases.content:
**Move the Turn Marker** — the game ends at the end of turn 12.

Remove **one First Strike Point** from the ASAT System box on a die roll of **6+**.
subPhases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** Next Turn (3.3.6) advances the game clock and resolves the slow decay of the Soviet ASAT System. The turn count is fixed: the game ends at the end of turn 12, which puts a hard horizon on every strategic decision and forces both sides to budget their resources against a known game length.

**What is at stake.** Two actions. Move the Turn Marker; the game ends at the end of turn 12 (3.3.6). Then roll one die against the ASAT System box in Tyuratam: on a 6+, remove one First Strike Point from that box (3.3.6).

**Gotchas.** New players sometimes treat the ASAT roll as flavor and forget it. It is not flavor. The ASAT System (9.1) penalizes NATO detection rolls by -1 per FSP present in Tyuratam, blocks Whitecloud and Snoopers Detect Raid card plays, and at 2 FSPs deducts 1 OPS from every NATO card played. The 6+ removal roll is the only routine way for that pressure to come off, so the Soviet player who has banked FSPs into ASAT should be aware that it is *not* permanent and may lose ground every turn. The game-end horizon is a planning rule: NATO cannot afford to play a 'next turn it will be better' game on turn 11. There is no turn 13.

**Synergies.** This subsection pairs with the Soviet player's FSP budgeting. ASAT is the cheapest FSP spend (just place the FSP) but it is the only one that decays, so on a long game it is a lower-priority allocation than nuclear weapons at sea or a strategic reserve step. It pairs with NATO's planning around card draws: holding a Whitecloud against a 1-FSP ASAT is a gamble that the 6+ roll fires before you have to spend the card.

**What the player can influence.** The roll itself is dice, but the *exposure* to it was a choice earlier in the game. Soviet players who pile FSPs into ASAT trust the slow decay; players who spend FSPs on Backfire reinforcement or Nuclear Weapons at Sea do not have FSPs sitting in Tyuratam to lose.

**Example beat.** End of Turn 9, both ASAT slots full with 2 FSPs. Soviet rolls the d10 for ASAT decay and rolls a 4: no FSP removed, ASAT stays at 2 and NATO continues to suffer -2 detection and -1 OPS per card. Turn marker advances to 10. NATO regroups, knowing there are only three turns left and the ASAT pressure is unlikely to lift in time.
subPhases.coachContentShort: The ASAT decay roll is not flavor: ASAT in Tyuratam costs NATO -1 detection per FSP, blocks Whitecloud and Snoopers Detect Raid card plays, and at 2 FSPs deducts 1 OPS from every NATO card (9.1). A 6+ roll removes one FSP, the only routine way that pressure comes off (3.3.6). The game ends after turn 12, so on turn 11 you cannot play 'next turn it will be better', every remaining FSP and Convoy must already be committed to a win condition.

phases.coachContent:
**Design intent.** The End of Turn Phase (3.3) is the bookkeeping and consequence beat. Everything the players did during Operations gets totaled into pressure on the European war, weather rolls forward, the deck cycles, and the turn marker advances. The phase reflects the design's view that naval play and the ground war are coupled: action at sea has to be paid out into the land tracks at a fixed cadence or the players would optimize the sea game in a vacuum.

**What is at stake.** Six subsections resolve in order (3.3.1 through 3.3.6): Turn Clean-Up, Invasions, First Strike, Weather, Event Cards, and Next Turn. Each is small in isolation; together they decide whether NATO loses ground, whether the Soviet player banks an FSP, whether next turn opens in Bad Weather, and what cards each side holds going forward.

**Gotchas.** The biggest mistake here is rushing. Resolving subsections out of order can break the math, particularly because the Invasion subsection (3.3.2) feeds the Capture Facilities sequence and the NATO nuke trigger, both of which depend on the war tracks being current. Players also forget the small upkeep items in Clean-Up (3.3.1): if a zone contains Fighter units of both sides, *all* Air Units in that zone return to base, not just the matching ones. The 3-hit removal on Europe South and the two Invasion Tracks (3.3.2) is mandatory, not optional, and missing it lets hits accumulate that should be wiped.

**Synergies.** This phase pairs with every track on the map. A turn where NATO holds back a Reaction card pairs with the Event Cards beat (3.3.5) because NATO can hold up to two cards (Soviet, one). A Soviet first-strike-icon turn pairs with sortie planning earlier in the turn to land SSBN Payload in First Strike zones in time for the 3.3.3 award.

**What the player can influence.** End of Turn is mostly upkeep, but two beats accept player choice: which cards to hold in 3.3.5 and which Norwegian-surrender bonus to take in 3.3.2 if applicable. Treat both as real decisions, not defaults.

**Example beat.** End of Turn 4 opens. Clean-Up returns NATO Phantoms from interception in North 5-6 to Lossiemouth. Invasions resolve: Soviet troops in Denmark trigger a 2-box advance on the Danish Invasion Track. First Strike fires, the turn shows the FS icon, Soviet SSBN Payload on station totals 6, the Soviet player gains 1 FSP. Weather rolls fresh and dumps Bad Weather into North 9-10. Event Cards: NATO holds 2, Soviet holds 1, both draw to 5. Turn marker advances to 5.
phases.coachContentShort: Resolve subsections 3.3.1 through 3.3.6 in strict order, the math depends on it: Invasions (3.3.2) feeds the Capture Facilities sequence and the NATO Ruhr nuke trigger, both of which need the war tracks current. The 3-hit removal on Europe South, Norway, and Denmark is mandatory, not optional. The only real player choices are which cards to hold (3.3.5) and which Norwegian surrender bonus to take if Norway has fallen.
